question: Air brakes are actually three different braking systems combined. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
choice_a: Hydraulic brake system
choice_b: Parking brake system
choice_c: Service brake system
choice_d: Emergency brake system
explanation: The manual states air brakes are really three systems: service brake, parking brake, and emergency brake. Hydraulic brakes are a separate, different braking technology used on cars and light/medium trucks.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, Introduction

question: Which braking system applies and releases the brakes when the driver uses the brake pedal during normal driving?
choice_a: The emergency brake system
choice_b: The service brake system
choice_c: The parking brake system
choice_d: The stab brake system
explanation: The service brake system applies and releases the brakes when you use the brake pedal during normal driving.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, Introduction

question: The emergency brake system in an air-braked vehicle is best described as which of the following?
choice_a: An entirely separate hydraulic backup system
choice_b: A device that only works on downgrades
choice_c: A system that uses parts of the service and parking brake systems to stop the vehicle if the brake system fails
choice_d: A system controlled solely by the alcohol evaporator
explanation: The emergency brake system uses parts of the service and parking brake systems to stop the vehicle in a brake system failure.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, Introduction

question: How is the air compressor typically connected to the engine?
choice_a: Through the transmission's clutch pack
choice_b: Through the alcohol evaporator
choice_c: Through a hydraulic hose
choice_d: Through gears or a v-belt
explanation: The air compressor pumps air into the air storage tanks and is connected to the engine through gears or a v-belt.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.1 Air Compressor

question: If the air compressor has its own oil supply separate from the engine, what should a driver do before driving?
choice_a: Check the oil level
choice_b: Drain the oil completely
choice_c: Replace the compressor belt
choice_d: Add alcohol to the reservoir
explanation: If the compressor has its own oil supply, the driver should check the oil level before driving.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.1 Air Compressor

question: What is the function of the air compressor governor?
choice_a: It cools the compressor with engine coolant
choice_b: It controls when the air compressor pumps air into the storage tanks
choice_c: It filters oil out of the compressed air
choice_d: It applies the spring brakes automatically
explanation: The governor controls when the air compressor will pump air into the air storage tanks, based on cut-in and cut-out pressures.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.2 Air Compressor Governor

question: At approximately what pressure does the governor's "cut-out" level stop the compressor from pumping air?
choice_a: Around 80 psi
choice_b: Around 100 psi
choice_c: Around 125 psi
choice_d: Around 150 psi
explanation: When air tank pressure rises to the cut-out level, around 125 psi, the governor stops the compressor from pumping air.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.2 Air Compressor Governor

question: At approximately what pressure does the governor's "cut-in" level allow the compressor to begin pumping air again?
choice_a: Around 55 psi
choice_b: Around 150 psi
choice_c: Around 125 psi
choice_d: Around 100 psi
explanation: When tank pressure falls to the cut-in pressure, around 100 psi, the governor allows the compressor to start pumping again.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.2 Air Compressor Governor

question: What is the purpose of air storage tanks in an air brake system?
choice_a: To hold compressed air so the brakes can be used several times even if the compressor stops working
choice_b: To warm the brake shoes before use
choice_c: To store alcohol for the evaporator
choice_d: To measure application pressure
explanation: Air storage tanks hold compressed air, providing enough air to allow the brakes to be used several times even if the compressor stops working.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.3 Air Storage Tanks

question: Why is it important to drain water and oil from air tanks?
choice_a: Water and oil are harmless and draining is only cosmetic
choice_b: Water can freeze in cold weather and cause brake failure
choice_c: Draining increases application pressure
choice_d: It prevents the governor from cutting out
explanation: Compressed air usually has water and compressor oil in it; the water can freeze in cold weather and cause brake failure, so tanks must be drained.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.4 Air Tank Drains

question: How are manually operated air tank drain valves typically opened?
choice_a: By pressing a foot pedal
choice_b: By using the parking brake control knob
choice_c: By turning a quarter turn or pulling a cable
choice_d: By flipping the wig wag arm
explanation: Manually operated drain valves are opened by turning a quarter turn or by pulling a cable, and must be drained at the end of each day of driving.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.4 Air Tank Drains

question: What feature can help prevent automatic air tank drains from freezing in cold weather?
choice_a: A safety relief valve
choice_b: A front brake limiting valve
choice_c: A stop light switch
choice_d: Electric heating devices
explanation: Automatic air tanks are available with electric heating devices to help prevent freezing of the automatic drain in cold weather.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.4 Air Tank Drains

question: What is the purpose of an alcohol evaporator in some air brake systems?
choice_a: To reduce the risk of ice forming in air brake valves and other parts during cold weather
choice_b: To lubricate the s-cam
choice_c: To cool the air compressor
choice_d: To increase application pressure
explanation: An alcohol evaporator puts alcohol into the air system to help reduce the risk of ice in air brake valves and other parts during cold weather, since ice can make the brakes stop working.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.5 Alcohol Evaporator

question: If a vehicle has an alcohol evaporator, is daily air tank drainage still required?
choice_a: No, the alcohol evaporator eliminates the need for drainage entirely
choice_b: Yes, daily drainage is still needed to get rid of water and oil, unless the system has automatic drain valves
choice_c: No, only weekly drainage is needed with an alcohol evaporator
choice_d: Yes, but only in the summer months
explanation: Daily air tank drainage is still needed to get rid of water and oil, unless the system has automatic drain valves.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.5 Alcohol Evaporator

question: Where is the safety relief valve installed in an air brake system?
choice_a: In the alcohol evaporator
choice_b: At the brake pedal
choice_c: In the first tank the air compressor pumps air to
choice_d: At the stop light switch
explanation: A safety relief valve is installed in the first tank the air compressor pumps air to, protecting the tank and system from too much pressure.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.6 Safety Valve

question: At approximately what pressure is the safety relief valve usually set to open?
choice_a: 125 psi
choice_b: 100 psi
choice_c: 55 psi
choice_d: 150 psi
explanation: The safety valve is usually set to open at 150 psi to protect the tank and system from too much pressure.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.6 Safety Valve

question: What should a driver do if the safety relief valve releases air?
choice_a: Have the fault fixed by a mechanic, since something is wrong
choice_b: Ignore it, as this is normal operation
choice_c: Add more alcohol to the evaporator
choice_d: Immediately drain all air tanks
explanation: If the safety valve releases air, something is wrong, and the fault should be fixed by a mechanic.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.6 Safety Valve

question: The brake pedal in an air brake system is also known by what other names?
choice_a: The wig wag or governor
choice_b: The foot valve or treadle valve
choice_c: The slack adjuster or power screw
choice_d: The tractor protection valve
explanation: The brake pedal is also called the foot valve or treadle valve; pushing it down harder applies more air pressure.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.7 The Brake Pedal

question: Why can pressing and releasing the brake pedal unnecessarily be a problem?
choice_a: It causes the alcohol evaporator to overflow
choice_b: It automatically triggers the safety relief valve
choice_c: It can let air out faster than the compressor can replace it, and if pressure gets too low the brakes won't work
choice_d: It permanently damages the s-cam
explanation: Releasing the brakes lets compressed air out of the system, reducing tank pressure. Pumping the pedal unnecessarily can let air out faster than the compressor can replace it, and if pressure gets too low, the brakes won't work.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.7 The Brake Pedal

question: What is the most common type of foundation brake?
choice_a: The wedge brake
choice_b: The air disc brake
choice_c: The power screw brake
choice_d: The s-cam drum brake
explanation: Foundation brakes are used at each wheel, and the most common type is the s-cam drum brake.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes

question: In an s-cam brake, what happens when the driver pushes the brake pedal?
choice_a: Air is let into each brake chamber, and air pressure moves the slack adjuster, twisting the camshaft and turning the s-cam to force the shoes against the drum
choice_b: A wedge is pushed directly between the ends of two brake shoes
choice_c: A power screw clamps the disc between brake lining pads
choice_d: Alcohol is released into the brake chamber
explanation: When you push the brake pedal, air is let into each brake chamber; air pressure pushes the rod out, moving the slack adjuster and twisting the brake camshaft, which turns the s-cam and forces the shoes against the drum.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes - S-cam Brakes

question: Why is this type of foundation brake called an "s-cam" brake?
choice_a: Because it was invented by a company named S-Cam Corp
choice_b: Because the camshaft component is shaped like the letter "S"
choice_c: Because it uses a spring-loaded system
choice_d: Because it is a safety-certified brake
explanation: The device is called the s-cam because it is shaped like the letter "S."
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes - S-cam Brakes

question: What happens when the driver releases the brake pedal on an s-cam brake?
choice_a: The safety valve opens automatically
choice_b: The alcohol evaporator refills
choice_c: The s-cam rotates back and a spring pulls the brake shoes away from the drum, letting the wheels roll freely
choice_d: The wedge locks the shoes in place
explanation: When you release the brake pedal, the s-cam rotates back and a spring pulls the brake shoes away from the drum, letting the wheels roll freely again.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes - S-cam Brakes

question: In a wedge brake, how does the brake chamber push rod apply the brakes?
choice_a: It turns a power screw that clamps a rotor
choice_b: It rotates an s-cam camshaft
choice_c: It releases alcohol into the drum
choice_d: It pushes a wedge directly between the ends of two brake shoes, shoving them apart against the drum
explanation: In a wedge brake, the brake chamber push rod pushes a wedge directly between the ends of two brake shoes, shoving them apart and against the inside of the brake drum.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes - Wedge Brakes

question: How many brake chambers can a wedge brake configuration have?
choice_a: A single chamber, or two chambers pushing wedges in at both ends of the brake shoes
choice_b: Only one chamber, never two
choice_c: Exactly four chambers per wheel
choice_d: No chambers; wedge brakes are purely mechanical
explanation: Wedge brakes may have a single brake chamber, or two brake chambers, pushing wedges in at both ends of the brake shoes.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes - Wedge Brakes

question: In air-operated disc brakes, what component is used instead of the s-cam?
choice_a: A wedge
choice_b: A power screw
choice_c: An alcohol evaporator
choice_d: A wig wag arm
explanation: In air-operated disc brakes, instead of the s-cam, a "power screw" is used; the brake chamber's pressure on the slack adjuster turns the power screw.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes - Disc Brakes

question: How does the power screw in an air disc brake apply the brakes?
choice_a: It rotates the brake drum directly
choice_b: It sprays alcohol on the rotor
choice_c: It clamps the disc or rotor between brake lining pads of a caliper, similar to a large c-clamp
choice_d: It releases the parking brake spring
explanation: The power screw clamps the disc or rotor between the brake lining pads of a caliper, similar to a large c-clamp.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes - Disc Brakes

question: Compared to s-cam brakes, how common are wedge brakes and disc brakes?
choice_a: They are equally common
choice_b: Wedge and disc brakes are more common than s-cam brakes
choice_c: Disc brakes have completely replaced s-cam brakes
choice_d: Wedge and disc brakes are less common than s-cam brakes
explanation: The manual states wedge brakes and disc brakes are less common than s-cam brakes.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes

question: What happens when the brake shoes and linings are pushed against the inside of the brake drum?
choice_a: This causes friction, which slows the vehicle and creates heat
choice_b: The alcohol evaporator activates
choice_c: The governor cuts out
choice_d: Nothing; friction only occurs on disc brakes
explanation: The brake shoes and linings pushed against the drum cause friction, which slows the vehicle and creates heat; too much heat can make the brakes stop working.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes

question: Where are brake drums located on a vehicle?
choice_a: Inside the air compressor
choice_b: On each end of the vehicle's axles, with wheels bolted to them
choice_c: Only on the front axle
choice_d: Inside the air storage tank
explanation: Brake drums are located on each end of the vehicle's axles, and the wheels are bolted to the drums.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes

question: What determines how much heat a brake drum can take without damage?
choice_a: The color of the drum
choice_b: The type of alcohol evaporator installed
choice_c: How hard and how long the brakes are used
choice_d: The cut-in pressure of the governor
explanation: The heat a drum can take without damage depends on how hard and how long the brakes are used.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.8 Foundation Brakes

question: How is the air compressor cooled?
choice_a: Only by a dedicated alcohol coolant
choice_b: It never requires cooling
choice_c: Only by a separate radiator
choice_d: It may be air cooled or cooled by the engine cooling system
explanation: The compressor may be air cooled or may be cooled by the engine cooling system.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.1 Air Compressor

question: What does the supply pressure gauge tell the driver?
choice_a: How much pressure is in the air tanks
choice_b: How much application pressure is on the front axle only
choice_c: The temperature of the brake drums
choice_d: The cut-out pressure of the governor
explanation: All vehicles with air brakes have a pressure gauge connected to the air tank that tells you how much pressure is in the air tanks.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.9 Supply Pressure Gauges

question: In a vehicle with a dual air brake system, how many supply pressure gauges (or gauge needles) are provided?
choice_a: None; dual systems do not use gauges
choice_b: One gauge for each half of the system, or a single gauge with two needles
choice_c: Exactly three, one per axle
choice_d: Only one gauge total, shared between both systems
explanation: If the vehicle has a dual air brake system, there will be a gauge for each half of the system, or a single gauge with two needles.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.9 Supply Pressure Gauges

question: What does the application pressure gauge show?
choice_a: How much air pressure is in the storage tanks
choice_b: The alcohol level in the evaporator
choice_c: How much air pressure the driver is applying to the brakes
choice_d: The governor's cut-in and cut-out settings
explanation: The application pressure gauge shows how much air pressure you are applying to the brakes; this gauge is not on all vehicles.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.10 Application Pressure Gauge

question: If the application pressure gauge shows increasing pressure needed to hold the same speed, what does this indicate?
choice_a: The governor has failed completely
choice_b: The alcohol evaporator needs refilling
choice_c: The supply pressure gauge is malfunctioning
choice_d: The brakes are fading, and the driver should slow down and use a lower gear
explanation: Increasing application pressure to hold the same speed means the brakes are fading; the driver should slow down and use a lower gear.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.10 Application Pressure Gauge

question: Besides brake fade, what other causes can lead to needing increased application pressure?
choice_a: Brakes out of adjustment, air leaks, or mechanical problems
choice_b: A fully-charged alcohol evaporator
choice_c: Cold weather alone, with no mechanical cause
choice_d: The tractor protection valve closing
explanation: The need for increased application pressure can also be caused by brakes out of adjustment, air leaks, or mechanical problems.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.10 Application Pressure Gauge

question: At what pressure must the low air pressure warning signal come on, at the latest, on a vehicle with air brakes?
choice_a: Before pressure falls below 100 psi
choice_b: Before pressure falls below 55 psi
choice_c: Before pressure falls below 125 psi
choice_d: Before pressure falls below 20 psi
explanation: A warning signal you can see must come on before the air pressure in the tanks falls below 55 psi (or one half the compressor governor cutout pressure on older vehicles).
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.11 Low Air Pressure Warning

question: On older vehicles, an alternate standard for the low air pressure warning is what?
choice_a: Twice the cut-in pressure
choice_b: 125 psi
choice_c: One half the compressor governor cutout pressure
choice_d: 150 psi
explanation: On older vehicles, the warning may instead be set at one half the compressor governor cutout pressure.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.11 Low Air Pressure Warning

question: What is the usual visual and audible form of the low air pressure warning?
choice_a: A blue light and a horn
choice_b: A green light only
choice_c: A siren only, no light
choice_d: A red light, and possibly a buzzer
explanation: The warning is usually a red light; a buzzer may also come on.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.11 Low Air Pressure Warning

question: What is the "wig wag" warning device?
choice_a: A device that drops a mechanical arm into the driver's view when pressure drops below 55 psi
choice_b: A gauge that shows application pressure
choice_c: A valve that cuts pressure to the front brakes in half
choice_d: A control knob that releases the parking brake
explanation: The wig wag device drops a mechanical arm into your view when the pressure in the system drops below 55 psi.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.11 Low Air Pressure Warning

question: What happens to an automatic wig wag arm once pressure rises back above 55 psi?
choice_a: It must be manually placed out of view
choice_b: It rises out of the driver's view automatically
choice_c: It stays in view permanently until serviced
choice_d: It triggers the safety relief valve
explanation: An automatic wig wag will rise out of your view when the pressure in the system goes above 55 psi.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.11 Low Air Pressure Warning

question: How does a manual reset wig wag differ from an automatic one?
choice_a: It resets itself every time the engine starts
choice_b: It only works on buses
choice_c: It must be placed in the "out of view" position manually, and will not stay in place until pressure is above 55 psi
choice_d: It uses a red light instead of a mechanical arm
explanation: The manual reset type wig wag must be placed in the "out of view" position manually, and it will not stay in place until the pressure in the system is above 55 psi.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.11 Low Air Pressure Warning

question: On large buses, at what pressure range is it common for the low pressure warning devices to signal?
explanation: On large buses it is common for the low pressure warning devices to signal at 80-85 psi.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.11 Low Air Pressure Warning

question: How does the air brake system's stop light switch work?
choice_a: It is an electric switch that works by air pressure and turns on the brake lights when the air brakes are applied
choice_b: It is a mechanical lever connected directly to the wheels
choice_c: It is triggered only by the parking brake control
choice_d: It is part of the alcohol evaporator system
explanation: The air brake system uses an electric switch that works by air pressure; the switch turns on the brake lights when you put on the air brakes.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.12 Stop Light Switch

question: Why must drivers behind a commercial vehicle be warned when it brakes?
choice_a: It is not required by the air brake system at all
choice_b: So they can be alerted through the electric stop light switch turning on the brake lights
choice_c: Only for vehicles without ABS
choice_d: Only when using the parking brake
explanation: Drivers behind you must be warned when you put your brakes on; the air brake system does this using an electric switch operated by air pressure that turns on the brake lights.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.12 Stop Light Switch

question: Which vehicles were typically equipped with a front brake limiting valve and control?
choice_a: Vehicles made after 1998
choice_b: Only buses built after 1997
choice_c: Vehicles made before 1975
choice_d: All modern vehicles with ABS
explanation: Some older vehicles, made before 1975, have a front brake limiting valve and a control in the cab.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.13 Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: The front brake limiting valve control is usually marked with which two positions?
choice_a: "On" and "off"
choice_b: "Fast" and "slow"
choice_c: "High" and "low"
choice_d: "Normal" and "slippery"
explanation: The control is usually marked "normal" and "slippery."
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.13 Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: What happens when the front brake limiting valve control is placed in the "slippery" position?
choice_a: It cuts the normal air pressure to the front brakes by half
choice_b: It doubles the pressure to the front brakes
choice_c: It shuts off the rear brakes entirely
choice_d: It activates the alcohol evaporator
explanation: When you put the control in the "slippery" position, the limiting valve cuts the "normal" air pressure to the front brakes by half.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.13 Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: According to the manual, what is true about front wheel braking and the effectiveness of limiting valves?
choice_a: Limiting valves increase stopping power and should always be used in the slippery position
choice_b: Front wheel braking is good under all conditions, and limiting valves actually reduce the vehicle's stopping power
choice_c: Front wheel skids from braking are common even on dry pavement
choice_d: Limiting valves are required equipment on all modern vehicles
explanation: Front wheel braking is good under all conditions; tests have shown front wheel skids from braking are not likely even on ice. Limiting valves actually reduce the stopping power of the vehicle.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.13 Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: For normal stopping power, in what position should a front brake limiting valve control be kept?
choice_a: "Slippery"
choice_b: It doesn't matter which position
choice_c: "Normal"
choice_d: "Off"
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to make sure the control is in the "normal" position to have normal stopping power.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.13 Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: Automatic front wheel limiting valves reduce air to the front brakes except under what condition?
choice_a: Except when the parking brake is engaged
choice_b: Except at speeds below 5 mph
choice_c: Except when the alcohol evaporator is empty
choice_d: Except when the brakes are put on very hard (55 psi or more application pressure)
explanation: Many vehicles have automatic front wheel limiting valves that reduce air to the front brakes except when the brakes are put on very hard (55 psi or more application pressure).
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.13 Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: Can the driver control automatic front wheel limiting valves?
choice_a: No, these valves cannot be controlled by the driver
choice_b: Yes, using the parking brake knob
choice_c: Yes, using the same cab control as older limiting valves
choice_d: Yes, but only while stationary
explanation: The manual states that automatic front wheel limiting valves cannot be controlled by the driver.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.13 Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: Why must trucks, truck tractors, and buses be equipped with emergency and parking brakes held on by mechanical force?
choice_a: Because mechanical force is required by the alcohol evaporator
choice_b: Because air pressure can eventually leak away
choice_c: Because electric switches are unreliable in cold weather
choice_d: Because hydraulic fluid can freeze
explanation: Emergency and parking brakes must be held on by mechanical force because air pressure can eventually leak away.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.14 Spring Brakes

question: How are spring brakes held off (released) during normal driving?
choice_a: By a mechanical latch
choice_b: By the alcohol evaporator
choice_c: By powerful springs held back by air pressure
choice_d: By the stop light switch
explanation: When driving, powerful springs are held back by air pressure. If the air pressure is removed, the springs put on the brakes.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.14 Spring Brakes

question: What happens if a leak in the air brake system causes all the air to be lost?
choice_a: The vehicle continues to operate with no brakes at all
choice_b: The wig wag arm resets
choice_c: The tractor protection valve opens fully
choice_d: The springs put on the brakes automatically
explanation: A leak in the air brake system, which causes all the air to be lost, will also cause the springs to put on the brakes.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.14 Spring Brakes

question: At what air pressure range will tractor and straight truck spring brakes come fully on?
choice_a: 20 to 45 psi (typically 20 to 30 psi)
choice_b: 55 to 80 psi
choice_c: 100 to 125 psi
choice_d: 0 to 10 psi only
explanation: Tractor and straight truck spring brakes will come fully on when air pressure drops to a range of 20 to 45 psi, typically 20 to 30 psi.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.14 Spring Brakes

question: When the low air pressure warning light and buzzer first come on, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Wait for the spring brakes to activate automatically before stopping
choice_b: Bring the vehicle to a safe stop right away, while brakes can still be controlled
choice_c: Continue driving normally until the next scheduled stop
choice_d: Immediately shift into the highest available gear
explanation: Do not wait for the brakes to come on automatically. When the low air pressure warning light and buzzer first come on, bring the vehicle to a safe stop right away, while you can still control the brakes.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.14 Spring Brakes

question: What does the braking power of spring brakes depend on?
choice_a: The type of alcohol evaporator installed
choice_b: The color of the parking brake knob
choice_c: The brakes being in adjustment
choice_d: The vehicle's speed at the time of application
explanation: The braking power of spring brakes depends on the brakes being in adjustment; if not properly adjusted, neither the regular brakes nor the emergency/parking brakes will work right.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.14 Spring Brakes

question: What does the parking brake control in the cab do to activate spring brakes?
choice_a: It adds air pressure to force the springs apart
choice_b: It directly activates the s-cam without using air
choice_c: It only functions when the alcohol evaporator is full
choice_d: It allows the driver to let the air out of the spring brakes, letting the springs put the brakes on
explanation: A parking brake control in the cab allows the driver to let the air out of the spring brakes, which lets the springs put the brakes on.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.14 Spring Brakes

question: In newer vehicles with air brakes, what shape and color is the parking brake control knob?
choice_a: A diamond-shaped, yellow, push-pull control knob
choice_b: A round, blue knob
choice_c: A square, green knob
choice_d: A triangular, red lever
explanation: In newer vehicles with air brakes, you put on the parking brakes using a diamond-shaped, yellow, push-pull control knob.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.15 Parking Brake Controls

question: How does a driver apply and release the parking brakes using the push-pull knob?
choice_a: Push in to apply, pull out to release
choice_b: Pull the knob out to apply the parking brakes, push it in to release them
choice_c: Turn the knob a quarter turn to apply
choice_d: Hold the knob halfway to apply
explanation: You pull the knob out to put the parking brakes (spring brakes) on, and push it in to release them.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.15 Parking Brake Controls

question: What caution does the manual give about pushing the brake pedal down while the spring brakes are on?
choice_a: It is always perfectly safe and recommended
choice_b: It is required to release the spring brakes
choice_c: It should never be done, as combined spring and air pressure forces could damage the brakes
choice_d: It only matters on vehicles built before 1975
explanation: Never push the brake pedal down when the spring brakes are on; the brakes could be damaged by the combined forces of the springs and the air pressure. It is best to develop the habit of not doing this even though some systems are designed to prevent it.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.15 Parking Brake Controls

question: What is a modulating control valve used for?
choice_a: To measure alcohol evaporator fluid levels
choice_b: To automatically drain the air tanks
choice_c: To cut front brake pressure in half
choice_d: To apply the spring brakes gradually, in case the service brakes fail
explanation: In some vehicles a control handle on the dash board may be used to apply the spring brakes gradually; this modulating valve lets you control the spring brakes if the service brakes fail.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.15 Parking Brake Controls

question: When parking a vehicle with a modulating control valve, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Move the lever as far as it will go and hold it in place with the locking device
choice_b: Leave the lever in the neutral position
choice_c: Disconnect the valve entirely
choice_d: Only move the lever halfway
explanation: When parking a vehicle with a modulating control valve, move the lever as far as it will go and hold it in place with the locking device.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.15 Parking Brake Controls

question: What is the purpose of a dual parking control valve system found on some buses?
choice_a: To double the stopping power of the vehicle
choice_b: To allow the driver to release the spring brakes temporarily using a separate air tank, so the vehicle can be moved in an emergency
choice_c: To eliminate the need for a parking brake entirely
choice_d: To connect the front and rear brake systems permanently
explanation: Some vehicles have a separate air tank which can release the spring brakes so you can move the vehicle in an emergency; pushing the control in releases the spring brakes using air from the separate tank.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.15 Parking Brake Controls

question: Why must a driver plan carefully when using the separate air tank to release spring brakes for moving the vehicle?
choice_a: The separate tank refills instantly
choice_b: It permanently disables the parking brakes
choice_c: There is only enough air in the separate tank to do this a few times
choice_d: It requires the engine to be off
explanation: There is only enough air in the separate tank to release the spring brakes a few times, so the driver must plan carefully or risk being stopped in a dangerous location when the air runs out.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.15 Parking Brake Controls

question: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after what date are required to have antilock brakes (ABS)?
choice_a: March 1, 1998
choice_b: January 1, 1994
choice_c: July 1, 2000
choice_d: March 1, 1997
explanation: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997 are required to be equipped with antilock brakes.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Other air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies) are required to have ABS if built on or after what date?
choice_a: March 1, 1998
choice_b: March 1, 1997
choice_c: January 1, 1975
choice_d: March 1, 2000
explanation: Other air brake vehicles - trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies - built on or after March 1, 1998 are required to be equipped with ABS.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What is ABS?
choice_a: A manual device for adjusting slack adjusters
choice_b: A computerized system that keeps your wheels from locking up during hard brake applications
choice_c: A type of foundation brake used only on trailers
choice_d: A backup hydraulic braking system
explanation: ABS is a computerized system that keeps your wheels from locking up during hard brake applications.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What color are the ABS malfunction lamps on tractors, trucks, and buses?
choice_a: Red
choice_b: Blue
choice_c: Yellow
choice_d: Green
explanation: Vehicles with ABS have yellow malfunction lamps; tractors, trucks, and buses will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the instrument panel.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Where are ABS malfunction lamps located on trailers?
choice_a: In the driver's cab dashboard
choice_b: On the right side, near the taillights only
choice_c: Underneath the vehicle, not visible externally
choice_d: On the left side, either on the front or rear corner
explanation: Trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Converter dollies manufactured on or after what date are required to have an ABS malfunction lamp?
choice_a: March 1, 1998
choice_b: March 1, 1997
choice_c: January 1, 1994
choice_d: July 1, 2017
explanation: Dollies manufactured on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have a lamp on the left side.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: On newer vehicles, when does the ABS malfunction lamp typically illuminate?
choice_a: Only when the ABS has failed
choice_b: At start-up for a bulb check, and then it goes out quickly
choice_c: Continuously while the vehicle is in motion
choice_d: Only above 55 mph
explanation: On newer vehicles, the malfunction lamp comes on at start-up for a bulb check, and then goes out quickly.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: If the ABS malfunction lamp stays on after the bulb check, or comes on once underway, what does this indicate?
choice_a: The alcohol evaporator is empty
choice_b: The parking brake is engaged
choice_c: The driver may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels
choice_d: Nothing of concern; this is normal
explanation: If the lamp stays on after the bulb check, or goes on once you are under way, you may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Does ABS increase or decrease a vehicle's normal braking capability?
choice_a: It significantly increases normal braking capability
choice_b: It significantly decreases normal braking capability
choice_c: It replaces normal braking capability entirely
choice_d: ABS is an addition to normal brakes; it does not decrease or increase normal braking capability
explanation: ABS is an addition to your normal brakes. It does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability; it only activates when wheels are about to lock up.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Does ABS necessarily shorten a vehicle's stopping distance?
choice_a: No, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking
choice_b: Yes, it always shortens stopping distance significantly
choice_c: Yes, but only above 55 mph
choice_d: No, ABS has no effect on braking at all
explanation: ABS does not necessarily shorten your stopping distance, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: How can a driver identify a towed unit's ECU to determine if it has ABS, when the unit predates ABS labeling requirements?
choice_a: By checking the odometer reading
choice_b: By looking under the vehicle for the electronic control unit and wheel speed sensor wires coming from the back of the brakes
choice_c: By checking the alcohol evaporator fluid color
choice_d: By testing the stop light switch
explanation: For towed units manufactured before ABS was required, look under the vehicle for the electronic control unit (ECU) and wheel speed sensor wires coming from the back of the brakes.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.1.16 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What is a dual air brake system?
choice_a: Two entirely separate vehicles sharing one brake pedal
choice_b: A system with two brake pedals
choice_c: Two separate air brake systems that use a single set of brake controls, each with its own air tanks, hoses, and lines
choice_d: A backup hydraulic system paired with an air system
explanation: A dual air brake system has two separate air brake systems, which use a single set of brake controls. Each system has its own air tanks, hoses, lines, etc.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.2 Dual Air Brake

question: In a typical dual air brake system, which axles does the "primary" system usually operate?
choice_a: The front axle only, always
choice_b: The trailer axles only
choice_c: No axles; it only operates the parking brake
choice_d: The rear axle or axles
explanation: One system typically operates the regular brakes on the rear axle or axles; this is called the "primary" system.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.2 Dual Air Brake

question: What is the "secondary" system in a dual air brake system?
choice_a: The system operating the front axle (and possibly one rear axle)
choice_b: The alcohol evaporator system
choice_c: A backup system only used in emergencies
choice_d: The system controlling the stop light switch only
explanation: The other system, called the "secondary" system, operates the regular brakes on the front axle (and possibly one rear axle).
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.2 Dual Air Brake

question: Before driving a vehicle with a dual air system, what minimum pressure should be built up in both the primary and secondary systems?
choice_a: 55 psi
choice_b: 100 psi
choice_c: 150 psi
choice_d: 125 psi
explanation: Before driving a vehicle with a dual air system, allow time for the air compressor to build up a minimum of 100 psi pressure in both the primary and secondary systems.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.2 Dual Air Brake

question: At what minimum value must the low air pressure warning light and buzzer shut off as pressure builds in both systems?
choice_a: Exactly 100 psi
choice_b: Exactly 20 psi
choice_c: A value set by the manufacturer that must be greater than 55 psi
choice_d: A value less than 55 psi
explanation: The warning light and buzzer should shut off when air pressure in both systems rises to a value set by the manufacturer, which must be greater than 55 psi.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.2 Dual Air Brake

question: If one air system in a dual system is very low on pressure while driving, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Continue driving normally since the other system will compensate fully
choice_b: Increase speed to reach a repair shop faster
choice_c: Switch the front brake limiting valve to slippery
choice_d: Bring the vehicle to a safe stop and have the air brake system fixed
explanation: If the warning light and buzzer come on while driving, you should stop right away and safely park the vehicle, then bring the vehicle to a safe stop and have the air brakes system fixed.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.2 Dual Air Brake

question: Why does most heavy-duty vehicles use a dual air brake system?
choice_a: For safety
choice_b: For fuel efficiency
choice_c: To reduce manufacturing cost
choice_d: To comply with alcohol evaporator regulations
explanation: Most heavy-duty vehicles use dual air brake systems for safety.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.2 Dual Air Brake

question: When checking slack adjusters on s-cam brakes, if the adjuster moves more than about how far where the push rod attaches, does it likely need adjustment?
choice_a: About six inches
choice_b: About one inch
choice_c: About one quarter inch
choice_d: Any movement at all
explanation: If a slack adjuster moves more than about one inch where the push rod attaches to it, it probably needs adjustment.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walk-around Inspection

question: To check slack adjusters, what should the driver do first?
choice_a: Drive at highway speed and apply the brakes hard
choice_b: Fill the alcohol evaporator
choice_c: Park on level ground, chock the wheels, and release the parking brakes so the slack adjusters can move
choice_d: Set the front brake limiting valve to slippery
explanation: Park on level ground and chock the wheels to prevent the vehicle from moving, then release the parking brakes so you can move the slack adjusters.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walk-around Inspection

question: What is described as the most common problem found in roadside inspections?
choice_a: Empty alcohol evaporators
choice_b: Failed stop light switches
choice_c: Cracked windshields
choice_d: Out-of-adjustment brakes
explanation: Out-of-adjustment brakes are the most common problem found in roadside inspections; vehicles with too much brake slack can be very hard to stop.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walk-around Inspection

question: All vehicles built since what year have automatic slack adjustors?
explanation: All vehicles built since 1994 have automatic slack adjustors.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walk-around Inspection

question: Even though automatic slack adjustors adjust themselves during full brake applications, what must a driver still do?
choice_a: Manually adjust them daily regardless of condition
choice_b: Still check them
choice_c: Replace them every 10,000 miles
choice_d: Nothing; they never need checking
explanation: Even though automatic slack adjustors adjust themselves during full brake applications, they must be checked.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walk-around Inspection

question: Why is manually adjusting an automatic slack adjuster considered dangerous?
choice_a: It voids the vehicle's warranty immediately
choice_b: It requires removing the wheel entirely
choice_c: It may give the driver a false sense of security about the effectiveness of the braking system, since it usually masks rather than fixes the underlying problem
choice_d: It is illegal in all circumstances
explanation: Manual adjustment of automatic slack adjusters is dangerous because it may give the driver a false sense of security, since it is likely the brake will soon be back out of adjustment as this procedure usually does not fix the underlying adjustment problem.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walk-around Inspection

question: What is recommended when brakes equipped with automatic adjusters are found to be out of adjustment?
choice_a: The driver should manually adjust them daily as routine maintenance
choice_b: The driver should ignore it since automatic adjusters self-correct within a day
choice_c: The driver should increase application pressure to compensate
choice_d: The driver should take the vehicle to a repair facility as soon as possible to have the problem corrected
explanation: It is recommended that when brakes equipped with automatic adjusters are found to be out of adjustment, the driver take the vehicle to a repair facility as soon as possible to have the problem corrected.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walk-around Inspection

question: What is the limit on crack length for brake drums or discs during inspection?
choice_a: Cracks must not be longer than one half the width of the friction area
choice_b: No cracks are allowed under any circumstance
choice_c: Cracks up to the full width of the friction area are acceptable
choice_d: Cracks are only a concern on disc brakes, not drums
explanation: Brake drums (or discs) must not have cracks longer than one half the width of the friction area.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walk-around Inspection

question: During the check of brake drums, linings, and hoses, what conditions in the linings (friction material) are unacceptable?
choice_a: Linings that are a different color than the drum
choice_b: Loose, soaked with oil or grease, or dangerously thin linings
choice_c: Linings with any visible wear at all
choice_d: Linings that make noise when the vehicle idles
explanation: Linings (friction material) must not be loose or soaked with oil or grease, and must not be dangerously thin.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.2 During Step 5 Walk-around Inspection

question: During Step 7 final air brake checks, at approximately what pressure should compressor pumping start (cut-in)?
choice_a: About 55 psi
choice_b: About 150 psi
choice_c: About 100 psi
choice_d: About 20 psi
explanation: Pumping by the air compressor should start at about 100 psi and stop at about 125 psi (check manufacturer's specifications).
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: During Step 7 final air brake checks, at approximately what pressure should compressor pumping stop (cut-out)?
choice_a: About 150 psi
choice_b: About 55 psi
choice_c: About 100 psi
choice_d: About 125 psi
explanation: Pumping by the air compressor should start at about 100 psi and stop at about 125 psi.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: How should a driver test the governor's cut-in pressure during the final air brake check?
choice_a: By running the engine at fast idle, then stepping on and off the brake with the engine idling to reduce tank pressure and see where the compressor cuts back in
choice_b: By checking the alcohol evaporator fluid level
choice_c: By fully applying the parking brake for one hour
choice_d: By disconnecting the air compressor drive belt
explanation: With the engine idling, step on and off the brake to reduce the air tank pressure; the compressor should cut-in at about the manufacturer's specified cut-in pressure, and the pressure should begin to rise.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: To test the air leakage rate with the engine off, what is the maximum acceptable pressure loss for a single vehicle?
choice_a: Less than three psi in one minute
choice_b: Less than two psi in one minute
choice_c: Less than five psi in one minute
choice_d: Less than one psi in one minute
explanation: With a fully-charged air system, turn off the engine, release the parking brake, and time the air pressure drop; the loss rate should be less than two psi in one minute for single vehicles.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: To test the air leakage rate with the engine off, what is the maximum acceptable pressure loss for a combination vehicle?
choice_a: Less than two psi in one minute
choice_b: Less than five psi in one minute
choice_c: Less than three psi in one minute
choice_d: Less than four psi in one minute
explanation: The loss rate should be less than three psi in one minute for combination vehicles (compared to less than two psi for single vehicles).
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: For the air leakage rate test with the engine off, what is a typical value for a "fully-charged" air system?
choice_a: Typically 55 psi
choice_b: Typically 20 psi
choice_c: Typically 100 psi
choice_d: Typically 125 psi
explanation: The air leakage rate test is performed with a fully-charged air system, typically 125 psi.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: For the applied brake leakage test (foot brake fully applied and held for one minute), what is the maximum acceptable pressure drop for a single vehicle?
choice_a: More than three psi is too much
choice_b: More than four psi is too much
choice_c: No drop whatsoever is acceptable
choice_d: More than ten psi is too much
explanation: Check the air gauge to see if the air pressure drops more than three pounds in one minute for a single vehicle; if so, the air loss rate is too much.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: For the applied brake leakage test (foot brake fully applied and held for one minute), what is the maximum acceptable pressure drop for a combination vehicle?
choice_a: More than two psi is too much
choice_b: More than four psi is too much
choice_c: More than three psi is too much
choice_d: More than six psi is too much
explanation: The air pressure should not drop more than four pounds in one minute for a combination vehicle during the applied brake leakage test.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: For the applied brake leakage test, at what pressure range should air be built up to governor cutoff before shutting off the engine?
explanation: With the air pressure built up to governor cutoff (120-140 psi), shut off the engine, chock the wheels if necessary, release the parking brake, and fully apply the foot brake.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: To test the low pressure warning signal, at what point must the signal come on?
choice_a: Only after the pressure drops below 20 psi
choice_b: Only when the vehicle exceeds 55 mph
choice_c: It is not required to be tested during inspection
choice_d: Before the pressure drops to less than 55 psi in the air tank (or tank with lowest pressure in dual systems)
explanation: The low air pressure warning signal must come on before the pressure drops to less than 55 psi in the air tank, or the tank with the lowest air pressure in dual air systems.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: What could happen in a single-circuit air system if the low air pressure warning signal doesn't work?
choice_a: Sudden emergency braking could occur without the driver knowing pressure was lost
choice_b: The vehicle would simply drive more slowly
choice_c: The alcohol evaporator would overflow
choice_d: The stop light switch would fail
explanation: If the warning signal doesn't work, the driver could lose air pressure without knowing it, which could cause sudden emergency braking in a single-circuit air system.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: To check that spring brakes come on automatically, at what pressure range should the tractor protection valve and parking brake valve close (pop out) on a combination vehicle?
choice_b: 20-45 psi (manufacturer's specification)
choice_d: 0-10 psi
explanation: The tractor protection valve and parking brake valve should close (pop out) when the air pressure falls to the manufacturer's specification, 20-45 psi, causing the spring brakes to come on.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: In dual air systems, the air pressure should build from what range within 45 seconds when the engine is at operating rpms?
choice_a: 50 to 90 psi
choice_b: 20 to 45 psi
choice_c: 85 to 100 psi
choice_d: 0 to 55 psi
explanation: When the engine is at operating rpms, the pressure should build from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds in dual air systems.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: In single air systems on pre-1975 vehicles, what is the typical requirement for pressure build-up?
choice_a: 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds
choice_b: 20 to 45 psi within 1 minute
choice_c: 100 to 125 psi within 10 seconds
choice_d: 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes at an idle speed of 600-900 rpm
explanation: In single air systems (pre-1975), typical requirements are pressure build-up from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes with the engine at an idle speed of 600-900 rpms.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: What should a driver do if air pressure does not build up fast enough during a buildup rate test?
choice_a: Not drive until the problem is fixed, since pressure may drop too low during driving and require an emergency stop
choice_b: Continue driving since it is not a serious issue
choice_c: Only drive on flat terrain until repaired
choice_d: Add more alcohol to the evaporator to compensate
explanation: If air pressure does not build up fast enough, pressure may drop too low during driving, requiring an emergency stop; don't drive until you get the problem fixed.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: How is the parking brake tested during the final air brake check?
choice_a: By checking the color of the control knob
choice_b: By stopping the vehicle, applying the parking brake, and gently pulling against it in a low gear to test that it holds
choice_c: By measuring supply pressure only, without moving the vehicle
choice_d: By fully applying the foot brake while parked
explanation: Stop the vehicle, put the parking brake on, and gently pull against it in a low gear to test that the parking brake will hold.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: How is the service brake test conducted during a final air brake check?
choice_a: By checking the alcohol evaporator level only
choice_b: By driving at highway speed and slamming the brakes
choice_c: By waiting for normal air pressure, releasing the parking brake, moving forward slowly (about 5 mph), and applying the brakes firmly while noting any pulling or delayed action
choice_d: By testing only while the vehicle is stationary
explanation: Wait for normal air pressure, release the parking brake, move the vehicle forward slowly (about five mph), and apply the brakes firmly, noting any vehicle pulling, unusual feel, or delayed stopping action.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.3 Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: During Step 2 engine compartment checks, what should a driver inspect if the air compressor is belt-driven?
choice_a: The alcohol evaporator fluid color
choice_b: The stop light switch wiring
choice_c: The parking brake knob shape
choice_d: The condition and tightness of the belt
explanation: If the air compressor is belt-driven, check the condition and tightness of the belt; it should be in good condition.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.3.1 During Step 2 Engine Compartment Checks

question: During a normal stop with air brakes, what should the driver do with a manual transmission before the vehicle stops?
choice_a: Not push the clutch in until the engine rpm is down close to idle
choice_b: Push the clutch in immediately as soon as the brake pedal is applied
choice_c: Shift into neutral before braking begins
choice_d: Push the clutch in and hold it throughout the entire stop
explanation: If you have a manual transmission, don't push the clutch in until the engine rpm is down close to idle; when stopped, select a starting gear.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.1 Normal Stops

question: In a vehicle without ABS, what happens when a driver brakes hard on slippery surfaces?
choice_a: The application pressure gauge automatically resets
choice_b: The wheels may lock up, causing loss of steering control or a skid, jackknife, or spin
choice_c: The spring brakes engage automatically at highway speed
choice_d: Nothing different happens compared to a vehicle with ABS
explanation: When you brake hard on slippery surfaces in a vehicle without ABS, your wheels may lock up; when your steering wheels lock up, you lose steering control, and other locked wheels can cause a skid, jackknife, or spin.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.2 Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: How does ABS help a driver during hard braking?
choice_a: It increases application pressure automatically
choice_b: It disables the parking brake
choice_c: It senses impending wheel lockup, reduces braking pressure to a safe level, and helps the driver maintain control
choice_d: It shuts off the engine to reduce speed
explanation: The ABS computer senses impending lockup, reduces the braking pressure to a safe level, and the driver maintains control; the driver may or may not stop faster, but should be able to steer around an obstacle.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.2 Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: How should a driver brake a tractor-trailer combination with ABS, compared to without ABS?
choice_a: Always brake much harder because ABS compensates fully
choice_b: Only apply light braking pressure at all times when ABS is present
choice_c: Disable ABS manually before braking hard
choice_d: Brake the same way, regardless of whether ABS is on the tractor, the trailer, or both
explanation: Brake the same way, regardless of whether you have ABS on the tractor, the trailer, or both; use only the braking force necessary to stop safely and stay in control.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.2 Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: What is the exception to normal ABS braking procedure described in the manual?
choice_a: If a driver always drives a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles, in an emergency stop, they can fully apply the brakes
choice_b: Drivers should never fully apply brakes even with ABS on all axles
choice_c: ABS should be disabled during rain
choice_d: There is no exception; the same rule always applies
explanation: There is only one exception: if you always drive a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles, in an emergency stop, you can fully apply the brakes.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.2 Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: If a vehicle's ABS malfunctions, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Stop the vehicle immediately and abandon the trip
choice_b: Drive normally, since regular brakes are still available, but get the system serviced soon
choice_c: Manually apply spring brakes for the remainder of the trip
choice_d: Disconnect the trailer immediately
explanation: If ABS malfunctions, you still have regular brakes; drive normally, but get the system serviced soon.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.2 Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: What two methods can a driver use for emergency stops to keep the vehicle in a straight line while allowing steering if necessary?
choice_a: Front limiting and rear limiting braking
choice_b: Governor braking and evaporator braking
choice_c: Controlled braking and stab braking
choice_d: Primary braking and secondary braking
explanation: You can use the "controlled braking" method or the "stab braking" method for emergency stops.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.3 Emergency Stops

question: What is the controlled braking method?
choice_a: Applying the brakes all the way and releasing only when wheels lock up
choice_b: Pumping the brake pedal rapidly and continuously
choice_c: Using only the parking brake to stop
choice_d: Applying the brakes as hard as possible without locking the wheels, keeping steering movements very small, and releasing if wheels lock or a larger steering adjustment is needed
explanation: With controlled braking, you apply the brakes as hard as you can without locking the wheels, keep steering wheel movements very small, and release the brakes if you need a larger steering adjustment or if the wheels lock, then re-apply as soon as you can.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.3 Emergency Stops

question: What is the stab braking method?
choice_a: Applying the brakes all the way, releasing when wheels lock up, then applying fully again as soon as the wheels start rolling
choice_b: Applying the brakes as hard as possible without ever locking the wheels
choice_c: Alternating between the parking brake and service brake repeatedly
choice_d: Only using the front brake limiting valve
explanation: Stab braking means applying the brakes all the way, releasing when the wheels lock up, and as soon as the wheels start rolling, applying the brakes fully again.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.3 Emergency Stops

question: During stab braking, how long can it take for the wheels to start rolling after the brakes are released?
choice_a: Up to ten seconds
choice_b: Up to one second
choice_c: Up to five minutes
choice_d: Instantaneously, with no delay
explanation: It can take up to one second for the wheels to start rolling after you release the brakes; if you re-apply before they start rolling, the vehicle won't straighten out.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.3 Emergency Stops

question: What is "brake lag" in an air brake system?
choice_a: The delay caused by the alcohol evaporator warming up
choice_b: The time it takes the governor to cut in
choice_c: The time required for the brakes to work after the brake pedal is pushed, due to the time for air to flow through the lines
choice_d: The delay between applying the parking brake and the spring brakes releasing
explanation: Brake lag is the added delay in air brakes; it takes a little time (one half second or more) for the air to flow through the lines to the brakes, unlike hydraulic brakes which work instantly.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.4 Stopping Distance

question: What are the four factors that make up total stopping distance for vehicles with air brakes?
choice_a: Perception Distance + Reaction Distance + Governor Distance + Braking Distance
choice_b: Reaction Distance + Braking Distance only
choice_c: Brake Lag Distance + Braking Distance only
choice_d: Perception Distance + Reaction Distance + Brake Lag Distance + Braking Distance
explanation: Total stopping distance equals Perception Distance + Reaction Distance + Brake Lag Distance + Braking Distance.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.4 Stopping Distance

question: At 55 mph on dry pavement, approximately how much distance does air brake lag add to stopping distance?
choice_a: About 32 feet
choice_b: About 100 feet
choice_c: About 10 feet
choice_d: About 450 feet
explanation: The air brake lag distance at 55 mph on dry pavement adds about 32 feet.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.4 Stopping Distance

question: For an average driver under good traction and brake conditions at 55 mph, approximately what is the total stopping distance?
choice_a: About 100 feet
choice_b: Over 450 feet
choice_c: About 200 feet
choice_d: About 32 feet
explanation: At 55 mph for an average driver under good traction and brake conditions, the total stopping distance is over 450 feet.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.4 Stopping Distance

question: How do hydraulic brakes, used on cars and light/medium trucks, compare to air brakes in terms of lag?
choice_a: Hydraulic brakes have more lag than air brakes
choice_b: Both have identical lag times
choice_c: Hydraulic brakes work instantly, while air brakes take a little time (one half second or more) for air to flow through the lines
choice_d: Hydraulic brakes have no braking distance factor at all
explanation: With hydraulic brakes, the brakes work instantly; with air brakes, it takes a little time (one half second or more) for the air to flow through the lines to the brakes.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.4 Stopping Distance

question: What causes brake fade, according to the manual?
choice_a: Cold weather causing the alcohol evaporator to freeze
choice_b: Low tire pressure
choice_c: The governor cutting out too early
choice_d: Excessive heat causing chemical changes in the brake lining that reduce friction, and expansion of the brake drums
explanation: Brake fade results from excessive heat causing chemical changes in the brake lining, which reduce friction, and also causes expansion of the brake drums.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.5 Brake Fading or Failure

question: As overheated brake drums expand, what happens to the brake shoes and linings?
choice_a: They have to move farther to contact the drums, and the force of contact is reduced
choice_b: They contract to compensate automatically
choice_c: They lock permanently against the drum
choice_d: They disengage from the s-cam entirely
explanation: As the overheated drums expand, the brake shoes and linings have to move farther to contact the drums, and the force of this contact is reduced.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.5 Brake Fading or Failure

question: What can happen if continued overuse of the service brakes increases brake fade too much?
choice_a: The alcohol evaporator automatically compensates
choice_b: The vehicle cannot be slowed down or stopped
choice_c: The application pressure gauge resets to zero
choice_d: The spring brakes disengage permanently
explanation: Continued overuse may increase brake fade until the vehicle cannot be slowed down or stopped.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.5 Brake Fading or Failure

question: Why is brake adjustment important to controlling brake fade across all wheels?
choice_a: Adjustment has no effect on fade, only on noise
choice_b: Only front brakes need adjustment to prevent fade
choice_c: Brakes out of adjustment stop doing their share of the work first, causing the other brakes to overheat and fade, reducing overall control
choice_d: Adjustment only matters for the parking brake
explanation: To safely control a vehicle, every brake must do its share of the work; brakes out of adjustment will stop doing their share before those that are in adjustment, and the other brakes can then overheat and fade.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.5 Brake Fading or Failure

question: On a long or steep downgrade, what role should the service brakes play relative to engine braking?
choice_a: The service brakes should be used exclusively, avoiding engine braking
choice_b: Engine braking should never be used on downgrades
choice_c: Spring brakes should be engaged continuously on downgrades
choice_d: The use of brakes is only a supplement to the braking effect of the engine, once the vehicle is in the proper low gear
explanation: The use of brakes on a long and/or steep downgrade is only a supplement to the braking effect of the engine; once the vehicle is in the proper low gear, follow the proper braking technique.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.6 Proper Braking Technique

question: On a downgrade, how hard should the brakes be applied according to proper braking technique?
choice_a: Just hard enough to feel a definite slowdown
choice_b: As hard as physically possible at all times
choice_c: Only lightly, barely touching the pedal
choice_d: Only using stab braking repeatedly
explanation: Apply the brakes just hard enough to feel a definite slowdown as part of the proper downgrade braking technique.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.6 Proper Braking Technique

question: When using proper downgrade braking technique, at what point should the driver release the brakes?
choice_a: Only when the vehicle comes to a complete stop
choice_b: When speed has been reduced to approximately five mph below the "safe" speed
choice_c: Immediately after applying them for one second
choice_d: Only when the low air pressure warning comes on
explanation: When your speed has been reduced to approximately five mph below your "safe" speed, release the brakes; this application should last about three seconds.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.6 Proper Braking Technique

question: In the manual's downgrade example, if the "safe" speed is 40 mph, at what speed does the driver reapply the brakes, and to what speed do they slow before releasing again?
choice_a: Apply at 45 mph, slow to 30 mph, then release
choice_b: Apply at 35 mph, slow to 20 mph, then release
choice_c: Apply at 40 mph, slow to 35 mph, then release
choice_d: Apply at 40 mph, slow to 25 mph, then release
explanation: If your safe speed is 40 mph, you would not apply the brakes until your speed reaches 40 mph, then apply hard enough to gradually reduce speed to 35 mph before releasing, repeating as necessary.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.6 Proper Braking Technique

question: If the low air pressure warning comes on while driving, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Continue driving until the spring brakes engage automatically
choice_b: Only slow down slightly and continue to the destination
choice_c: Ignore it unless the buzzer also sounds
choice_d: Stop and safely park the vehicle as soon as possible, since there might be an air leak
explanation: If the low air pressure warning comes on, stop and safely park your vehicle as soon as possible; there might be an air leak in the system.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.7 Low Air Pressure

question: Why is it safer to stop while there is still enough air in the tanks to use the foot brakes, rather than waiting for the spring brakes to engage?
choice_a: A heavily loaded vehicle will take a long distance to stop because spring brakes don't work on all axles, and lightly loaded or slippery-road vehicles may skid out of control when spring brakes engage
choice_b: Spring brakes apply too gently to be effective
choice_c: The parking brake control knob is unreliable
choice_d: Spring brakes only work above 55 mph
explanation: A heavily loaded vehicle will take a long distance to stop because the spring brakes do not work on all axles; lightly loaded vehicles or vehicles on slippery roads may skid out of control when the spring brakes come on. It is much safer to stop while there is enough air to use the foot brakes.
source_note: New Hampshire Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 5 - Air Brakes, 5.4.7 Low Air Pressure

question: While driving with low air pressure but before the spring brakes fully engage, when is controlled braking still possible?
choice_a: Only after the spring brakes have already engaged
choice_b: Only while enough air remains in the air tanks
choice_c: Never; controlled braking requires full tank pressure
choice_d: Only when the parking brake control is pulled
explanation: Controlled braking is possible only while enough air remains in the air tanks.
